text.text_excerpt: Everyone likes to throw around the term "dive bar", but what really constitutes a dive? If I asked you to describe one, you might start to picture an old building where maintenance has been neglected, a bathroom that even the grizzliest street punk might hesitate to enter. Maybe a ratty old couch tucked away in a dark corner whose previous owners had Greek letters on their shirts, or a smelly dog wandering around occasionally sniffing at your heels as you sit at the bar and sip on the cheapest of the cheap. The bar itself, of course, would be made out of plywood and milk crates and power for the lighting would be provided by a group of guinea pigs rowing a boat in a open fish tank. Okay, ...

This is one of my absolute favorite music venues in the entire city. In fact, Banks St. Bar is my second favorite music venue (number one is Saturn Bar, for the acoustics and "balcony" seating) in New Orleans. Every single time I've been here, I've seen an incredible show. Granted, I've only been to Banks St. Bar five or six times over the last few years, but every single time has been remarkable. My first show was some sort of surf rock band. Since then, I've been to a live filming of a death metal concert (for some low budget film about, well, a death metal band), a gorgeous solo set by Micah McKee (of Silent Cinema/Empress Hotel/Little Maker), and a face melting show with local ska ban...

This is a comfortable Mid-city bar with a basic dive feel. The bartenders rock, and won;t shy away from conversation. Plenty of live music (most nights) fills the bar, so if there's a band you won't be able to converse. A bit dirty and not well-lit, Banks Street doesn't try that hard and doesn't expect you to. Really friendly place.
